Akassa Corn Porridge

Served at: Fete du Vodoun (Benin Vodoun Festival)

Serves 4-6Prep 10 minCook 25 min

Akassa is a staple, firm corn porridge or paste, deeply embedded in the culinary traditions of Benin, particularly during the Fete du Vodoun. It serves as a neutral, satisfying base, traditionally accompanying rich, flavorful sauces and stews that are central to festive meals and offerings.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups (240g) fine corn flour or cornstarch
  • 6 cups (1.4 liters) water, divided
  • Pinch of salt (optional)

Method

  1. In a medium bowl, whisk together 1 cup (240ml) of cold water with the corn flour (or cornstarch) until a smooth, lump-free slurry is formed.
  2. Bring the remaining 5 cups (1.2 liters) of water to a rolling boil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over high heat.
  3. Reduce the heat to medium-low. Slowly pour the corn flour slurry into the boiling water in a steady stream, whisking continuously to prevent any lumps from forming.
  4. Switch to a sturdy wooden spoon or spatula and continue stirring vigorously. The mixture will begin to thicken rapidly.
  5. Keep stirring and cooking for about 15-20 minutes, pressing the mixture against the sides of the pot to ensure it cooks evenly and becomes very smooth and firm. The Akassa is ready when it pulls away from the sides of the pot and has a uniform, thick consistency.
  6. Remove the pot from the heat.
  7. To serve, you can either spoon portions directly onto plates, or for a traditional presentation, moisten your hands with water and quickly shape the hot Akassa into smooth, small balls or patties.
  8. Serve immediately alongside your favorite West African sauce or stew.

Tips

  • For a more authentic, slightly tangy flavor, you can traditionally ferment the corn flour by mixing it with water and letting it sit at room temperature for 1-2 days before cooking.
  • Akassa is best enjoyed with savory accompaniments like groundnut stew, tomato-based sauces with fish or meat, or various vegetable stews.
  • Constant stirring during the cooking process is crucial to prevent lumps and ensure a smooth texture, as well as to prevent the porridge from sticking to the bottom of the pot.
